summary:
The Republic of the Marshall Islands has no criminalisation regime covering consensual same-sex conduct. Human Dignity Trust dates decriminalisation to 2005, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sex or sexual orientation, so a visitor faces no statutory offence for consensual sex and no differential age threshold.

The Gender Equality Act 2019 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and sexual orientation across all areas, naming the political, legal, economic, employment, social and domestic spheres. It obliges the government to adopt measures eliminating stereotypes, prejudice and harmful practices on those grounds, and establishes a programme to sensitise judicial and law enforcement officers and other public officials. Before 2019 no legal protection against discrimination on gender identity or sexual orientation existed in employment or in the provision of goods and services.

The Code of Judicial Conduct 2008 provides that a judge shall not manifest bias, prejudice or harassment based on sexual orientation, and shall require lawyers to refrain from such bias, prejudice or harassment.

Same-sex marriages and civil unions are not recognised, and households headed by same-sex couples are ineligible for the protections available to opposite-sex married couples. The Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1988 does not expressly prohibit same-sex marriage, but section 428(1) assumes opposite-sex parties, setting minimum ages of 18 for the male and 16 for the female. Whether constitutional or statutory non-discrimination guarantees on sexual orientation, marital status and family status confer a right to marry remains unresolved, as the Supreme Court has yet to rule.

On 22 March 2011 the Marshall Islands joined the Human Rights Council joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity, which expressed concern at killings, rape, torture and criminal sanctions on those grounds. In 2016 the country received recommendations from Germany and Israel to prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation.

The 2015 US State Department Human Rights Report on the Marshall Islands listed prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence as significant problems, and recorded no reports of torture, arbitrary killings, disappearances or LGBT-specific abuses.
tangentialFactors: The Pacific Sexual & Gender Diversity Network profiles Anfernee Nenol Kaminaga, 25, a pansexual genderqueer Marshallese person who co-created and led Brighten the Rainbow, regarded as the first openly LGBTIQ initiative in the Marshall Islands. Kaminaga is also a UNESCO Youth Ambassador and a youth representative at the first UN Youth Climate Action Summit.
